newsitem.title: TURKEY: S.African gold miners see output fall in 1996.
newsitem.headline: S.African gold miners see output fall in 1996.

text.p: Gold miners of South Africa, the world's main gold producing country, said on Wednesday they were expecting output for this year to fall to about 500 tonnes from 522 tonnes last year in line with a decline in productivity and pressure from prices and costs.

"Gold production in 1995 fell to 522 tonnes, a 12 percent decline on the previous year," said Tom Main, chief executive of Chamber of Mines of South Africa. "We expect the figure in 1996 to decline further to around 500 tonnes," he told the International Gold Markets conference in Istanbul.

London-based Economic Intelligence Unit specialist Alan Mackie said earlier at the conference that the South African decline in output would squeeze global gold production as a capacity of about 60 tonnes per year of the country would be slated out of production in the next five years.

Main said a fall in productivity and rapidly increasing costs and "constant" gold prices had increased pressure on high- cost older mines, which are most vulnerable to closure due to their limited grade flexibility.
"The development of new marketing and pricing strategies has become more important for South African gold producers if they are to maximise profits in the current environment," he said.

He said South African producers were following a passive pricing doctrine, relying on the cushion of substantial profit to revenue ratios rather than risk losing upside gains, "which tend to be highly leveraged for the producers."
South African miners are forced to practice hedging as an important alternative price insurance device in an era of declining production and rapidly increasing costs, he said.
"Hedging is one way to...enable meaningful strategic planning to take place in what is inherently a risky environment," he said.

"Producers are by nature long gold by virtue of the massive capital investment required to bring an orebody to account and the subsequent burden of operating costs...Hedging is not a sign of pessimism but an alternative method for managing risk."

Hedging would help producers maximise their returns over the long term, prolong the profitable production life of a mine and lock in a gold price that is adequate to cover the costs of a particular development such as a new shaft, Main said.
Analysts said South Africa's production costs have risen significantly in past years, making it the country with the highest cost of production in the world.

Stewart Murray, chief executive of Gold Fields Mineral Service company, told the conference South African costs, which rose significantly during the 1993-95 period due to the strength of the rand against the dollar, had fallen in the second quarter of this year.

"This year there has been a dramatic decline in the currency's value, which accounted for the drop in costs during the second quarter. Costs in rand terms actually rose by four percent in that quarter," he said.

Main said gold spot price, local interest rates, gold price volatility, gold lease rates and exchange rate fluctuations were the five risk factors that would drive South African producers' pricing strategy.
He said gold mining would enjoy a "renaissance" in South Africa, which has about 40 percent of the world's recoverable gold reserves, if cost and revenue constraints improved as in the past.
"I can emphatically refute the view that the South African gold mining industry is about to be laid to rest," he said.
